You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

It seems I'm expected to expand the bottom-left through the bottom-right mask using the counts from the upper quadrants. I'm curious if this problem is similar to what I’ve described before regarding ARC grids. It feels like I'm on the right track!**Analyzing quadrant stencils**

I need to think about filling and expanding the bottom-right quadrant stencil using data from the bottom-left. In this case, the bottom-right has repetitive horizontal stripes as a stencil, while the bottom-left consists entirely of ones. 

It’s interesting how these patterns can guide the transformation process. I'm pondering how to effectively apply this stencil technique for a coherent output, ensuring I capture the essence of the matrices involved. I feel like I'm gradually piecing this together!

arc_color1_color6_boundary_marking ARC: Color-1/color-6 boundary marking with color 7 
 For ARC grids matching the demonstrated setup—background 8, color-1 shapes, and a color-6 marker at the upper-right, with output color 7—first check whether the color-1 structure forms a full-height divider. In the non-separating cases (demos 2 and 3 and the solved test), preserve all 1 and 6 cells; recolor to 7 the accessible outer-frame 8 cells and the one-cell 8-neighbor exterior around color-1 components connected to the grid boundary. Leave unrelated interior 8 cells and isolated interior 1 objects unchanged. Distinct divider exception: when a full-height 1 divider separates the 6-side region, keep the divider, clear objects on the opposite side as shown in the demo, and fill the 6-side region with 7. Treat this as a narrow pattern-specific rule; verify the structure against examples before applying, and do not generalize it to unrelated grids. 

arc_quadrant_mask_expansion ARC: Expand bottom-left source through bottom-right mask using top-quadrant counts 
 For even-sized ARC grids that visibly divide into four equal quadrants, consider this rule only when the upper quadrants encode output dimensions and the lower quadrants form a source-and-mask pair. Count nonzero cells in the top-left quadrant for output height and in the top-right quadrant for output width. Use the bottom-left as the source and the bottom-right as a block mask: expand each source cell into a bottom-right-sized block, preserving nonzero mask colors and replacing mask zeros with that source cell's color, then crop to the counted output dimensions. If the bottom-right is entirely zero, the demonstrated variant is a direct crop of the bottom-left. Confirm the quadrant roles and output dimensions against examples before applying. 

arc_quadrant_stencil_fill_and_expand ARC: Fill and expand a bottom-right quadrant stencil from bottom-left data 
 For ARC inputs visibly divided into equal quadrants, consider whether the bottom-right quadrant is a repeating stencil whose zero cells are filled using the bottom-left quadrant. Confirm this structure against demonstrations before applying. In the demonstrated solid-data case, the bottom-left quadrant is a single solid color: tile the bottom-right pattern with its zero cells filled by that color, then crop to height equal to the count of nonzero cells in the top-left quadrant and width equal to the count of nonzero cells in the top-right quadrant. In the demonstrated varying-data case, bottom-left values supply fill colors for repeated bottom-right stencil tiles, producing an expanded output (the 8x8-to-16x16 example). A solved test had 16 ones in the top-left, 4 fives in the top-right, solid 9 in the bottom-left, and a 3/0 checkerboard stencil; its output was a 16x4 checkerboard of 3 and 9. One demo with an all-zero bottom-right produced the bottom-left pattern as output, but treat that only as an observed fallback, not a general rule. 

arc_fill_between_parallel_diagonal_stroke_segments ARC: Fill between parallel diagonal stroke segments 
 For ARC grids with background 8 and sparse same-color diagonal strokes on lines r+c=s, apply this rule only when that parallel-diagonal structure is present. Split each line into maximal contiguous segments. Represent each segment by its s value and its endpoint interval in v=r-c. For each integer v, find the segments whose intervals contain v, sort them by s, and fill background-8 cells strictly between each consecutive pair with color 2. Preserve all input strokes. This rule matched demonstrations with source colors 4 and 6 and solved a test with source color 7. 

arc_marker_guided_chebyshev_region_layers ARC: Marker-guided coloring of barrier-separated regions with 8-neighbor layers 
 For ARC grids with a uniform background partitioned by line barriers and marker colors placed at successive inner boundary layers, first confirm this structure from the examples. Preserve barrier cells. Treat each 4-connected free region independently, find its boundary cells (adjacent by king move to a barrier or the grid exterior), and compute inward distance layers using 8-neighbor/king-move propagation within that region. Use the marker colors at successive depths as a cyclic color sequence for the layers, preserving any marker cells if the examples require it. A 4-neighbor BFS layer fill failed on the irregular region in task-9a643f12; the 8-neighbor layer version solved it. Apply only when examples confirm this rule, not as a general rule for arbitrary regions. 

arc_repack_solid_and_hollow_square_tiles ARC: Repack solid and hollow square tiles into sorted columns 
 For ARC grids containing repeated same-sized solid and hollow square tiles on a background, first verify the tile dimensions and that the objects separate into solid and hollow categories. Preserve each tile's cell pattern and color. Sort each category independently by its original top-to-bottom position. Build the output with hollow tiles in the left column and solid tiles in the right column, one tile per tile-height band; align category items by their sorted index and pad any missing tile with background. Infer output dimensions from the number of bands needed by the longer category. Apply only when the demonstrated structure fits. 

arc_components_into_matching_bands Transfer components into matching horizontal bands (general, v2) 
 For ARC grids with a uniform-background upper workspace containing colored shapes and lower horizontal bands with distinct interior-fill and side-marker colors, process each upper-workspace foreground 4-connected component independently—even when different colors together form one visual motif. Match a component to a lower band when the component's color equals that band's interior-fill color. Project only that component's mask into the matching band at the same columns, bottom-align its bounding box within the band's height, and recolor its cells to the band's side-marker/border color. Leave all other cells in the component's bounding box as the band's fill color, preserve the band and unrelated cells, and clear the original foreground components from the upper workspace. Different colors within one motif can therefore populate different bands. Do not treat a whole multicolor template as one object or recolor its full bounding box. This rule was validated by two demonstrations and a correct solution for task-7c173794; an initial whole-template recoloring guess was incorrect.
